correctness.rationale: The exact residual line search is an orthogonal rank-one projection. Independent direction angles give a stationary 1-dependent sequence of logarithmic cosine factors; its law is a Poisson kernel with parameter q, and adjacent-difference law has parameter q squared. Strong law/1-dependent CLT apply because logarithmic singularities have finite moments. Fourier/Poisson averaging yields drift 2 log((1+q squared)/2) and an explicit variance computed through the disk automorphism and dilogarithm covariance identity. A standalone checker reproduces exact symbolic fourth-moment characteristic polynomial and independently integrates the drift/variance/covariance for seven q values and simulates four Gaussian systems. Initial residual direction only contributes one finite term.

originality.rationale: The closest accessible prior calculation provides exact MEAN-SQUARE planar Gaussian projection rate, not an almost-sure logarithmic exponent or a 1-dependent dilogarithmic CLT variance. The source iterative-refinement paper supplies exact line search with nondivergence and sufficient correction accuracy, but its stated claims do not cover independent uninformative corrections or their pathwise fluctuations. Random Pursuit offers expected convergence rates but not this exact CLT. Multiple Index searches for equivalent random-projection, Lyapunov and angle-log expressions found no covering result; unindexed or implicit derivations remain a risk.
residual_risks: Exact formula may have an equivalent unindexed historical expression under products of random rank-one projections, Poisson-kernel angle processes, or log-cosine observables.

value.rationale: The relevant algorithmic gap is what exact residual line search achieves when basic correction directions are completely uninformative and correction-accuracy hypotheses fail. Almost-sure exponential convergence and a closed q-dependent fluctuation law quantify typical trajectories and uncertainty, while the known mean-square rate demonstrably misrepresents the typical rate. Explicit dilogarithmic covariance and CLT are nontrivial mathematically motivated distributional information rather than a routine one-step inequality or numerical recomputation.
